t: Lonely Pixel II — Row Signatures and Counting
o: We must count 'B' cells at (r, c) where row r has exactly `target` black pixels, column c has exactly `target` black pixels, and every row containing a black pixel in column c is identical to row r. In example 1, columns 1 and 3 each have 3 black pixels, all lying in identical rows 0–2 (each with exactly 3 B's), giving 3 + 3 = 6. In example 2, each column has 3 black pixels but target = 1, so nothing qualifies. With m, n ≤ 200, an O(m·n) or O(m·n·something small) approach easily fits; the challenge is checking the "identical rows" rule efficiently rather than comparing rows repeatedly.
k: Precompute per-row black counts and group rows by their exact content signature so equality checks are O(1).
For a valid pixel, every black pixel in its column must belong to rows that are all identical to row r — so the count of such rows equals the column's black count.
A single pass over columns using a hash map of row signatures yields an O(m·n) solution.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Row Comparison
a.i: For each black pixel (r, c), directly verify both rules: count blacks in row r and column c, then compare row r against every other row that has a black pixel in column c. This is straightforward but repeats work heavily — each candidate may trigger up to m full-row comparisons of length n.
s: Iterate over every cell; skip non-'B' cells.
Count black pixels in row r and column c; if either differs from target, continue.
For every row i with picture[i][c] == 'B', check it equals row r element-wise; if any differs, reject this pixel.
If all checks pass, increment the answer.
a.t: O(m^2 · n^2) — for each of up to m·n candidates we do O(m·n) counting/comparison work. Fine for m, n ≤ 200 but wasteful.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input.

a.n: Approach 2: Precomputed Counts + Row Signature Map (Optimal)
a.i: Key observation: if column c has exactly `target` black pixels and all of them lie in rows identical to row r, then there are exactly `target` such identical rows, and each contributes one lonely pixel in column c. So instead of validating each pixel, we can process column by column: collect the set of rows having a black pixel in column c; if that set's size equals target and all rows in it share the same signature, add target to the answer. Grouping rows by a string/hashable signature makes equality checks O(1) after O(m·n) preprocessing.
s: Compute rowCount[r] = number of 'B' in row r for all rows.
Build a map from each row's string signature to its list of row indices (or just use signatures for comparison).
For each column c, gather indices of rows with picture[i][c] == 'B'.
If that count equals target and all those rows have identical signatures (and rowCount matches target, implied by identical rows), add target to the answer.
a.t: O(m·n) — building signatures, counts, and column lists is linear in the matrix size; the final loop touches each black pixel once plus O(target) signature comparisons per qualifying column, bounded by O(m·n) overall.
a.sp: O(m·n) — storing each row as a string plus column index lists.

w: In an interview, mention the brute force briefly, then lead with the signature-map approach since it collapses the expensive row-equality checks into hashing. Pitfalls: forgetting that when a column qualifies, **all** target pixels in it count (hence adding `target`, not 1); forgetting the row-count rule is automatically satisfied by identical rows only if those rows themselves contain exactly `target` blacks — since identical rows have equal counts and the column check gives target blacks among them, verifying `sigCount >= target` plus identical signatures suffices, but be careful with rows outside the column that share the signature. Edge cases: target larger than any row/column count (answer 0), all-white grids, and duplicate identical rows. Follow-ups: handle streaming updates to the grid, or generalize to k colors.
